doc.title: Chuck Findley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 6, 2023

title: Playing the Paderewski's supper club in Cleveland
summary: At sixteen he took over the trumpet-and-rhythm gig at Paderewski's, and substituted wrong bridges to a pianist who couldn't improvise.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Of course. You have to come back to make some sense to it, you don’t want them to leave if you’re playing a live concert, a live performance. You know it’s like, and growing up I played in Cleveland, and I played in this one band it was called, well the club was called — well the club was called Paderewski’s and it was, the family was related to Ignace Paderewski from Poland — the famous composer. And I think he was the minister of something in Poland, Warsaw. But the family was Polish and it was called Paderewski’s and it was a rhythm section and the mother and the father, they did a show too and they sang and comedy and all that kind of stuff you know. And it was just trumpet and rhythm section. Well my brother had the gig first. And it was five nights a week — it was a nice supper club. And he had it first and then in Cleveland Gary Barone, I don’t know if you know Gary Barone and the Barone brothers, Mike Barone and Gary Barone who is a trumpet player, and he is older, he is in between my brother’s age and my age. And my brother left that gig and Gary did it. And then after Gary I got the gig. So I was sixteen and I’m playing. But what was great about it was we’d play all these tunes. I mean you name it, “Moon Over Miami,” you know “Poor Butterfly,” God I can go on and on and on. But I learned all these tunes. I knew a lot of them from playing Music Minus One which I did. I did that a lot and it was great. But I’m playing these tunes but when it would get to the bridge a lot of times I wouldn’t remember the bridge. So I would play another bridge. Well Jan Paderewski, the piano player, it was his band. He was a wonderful piano player but he only knew the tunes in the keys they were © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

written in and that’s it. He could not improvise whatsoever. So it was just — so when I’d go into a bridge for another tune he was completely lost, he goes like what’s he doing or what’s going on. And then I’d come out of that eight into the last eight of the tune, into the melody of the song we were playing. You know I wasn’t improvising I just played another bridge because I didn’t know it at the time.

Yeah I was. But you know what? It was a great experience, it really was. To this day, sometimes but I mean when you think about it, now think about all these tunes, you could play so many bridges are so similar, it goes back to the, you know to the last eight of the tune so I mean, I mean, well you know exactly what I’m talking about.
